title: Pipes, Filters, and One Direction
gist: Two component types and one rule about direction. It is the architecture behind every Unix shell pipeline, every ETL tool and every Step Function — and its whole value comes from what it refuses to let filters do.
minute: Two components only. **Filters** hold functionality — stateless, one task each. **Pipes** carry data between them, **one-way and point-to-point**.
Four filter types: **producer** (the source), **transformer** (`map`), **tester** (`reduce` — test and optionally forward), **consumer** (the termination point).
Technically partitioned, quantum of 1, usually monolithic. Its strengths are **cost, simplicity and modularity**; any filter can be replaced without touching the others.
The risks are all boundary risks: **overloaded filters**, **bidirectional communication**, unclear **error exits** from a running pipeline, and **contract changes** between filters.

Use it for **distinct, ordered, deterministic one-way steps**. For non-deterministic workflows, use event-driven architecture instead — piling tester filters into a pipeline to fake it wrecks maintainability.

sections.alt: Producer, transformer, tester and consumer filters joined by one-way pipes
sections.cap: Fig. 12-1 · the isomorphic shape: one deployment unit, functionality in filters, unidirectional pipes.
sections.p: Pipes carry any data format, though architects favour small payloads for performance. If filters are deployed as separate services, the pipe becomes a one-way remote call — REST, messaging, streaming. Either way, monolithic or distributed, pipes can be synchronous or asynchronous; in a monolith, asynchrony means threads or embedded messaging.
quotes: tr -cs A-Za-z '\n' | tr A-Z a-z | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | sed ${1}q

Donald Knuth was asked to print the *n* most frequent words in a file, sorted by frequency. He wrote ten-plus pages of Pascal and designed a new algorithm along the way. McIlroy answered with six shell filters. The composability is the point of the style.

sections.alt: Four filters in sequence, three of them writing to their own databases
sections.cap: Most pipelines are monolithic with one database. Nothing in the style requires that.
sections.p: This one is a continuous fitness function running in production against an operational characteristic. Note the separation: **Capture Raw Data** knows only how to subscribe and receive; **Duration** (a tester) knows only how to qualify data and decide whether to forward it; **Duration Calculator** knows only the calculation. Change the calculation and no other filter moves.

sections.t: Two filters need to talk back and forth
sections.alt: Two filters with a forward pipe and a crossed-out return pipe
sections.sit: Filter B needs something back from filter A mid-processing. The obvious fix is to let the pipe carry a response, or add a second pipe going the other way.
opts: Add the return pipe. It's one exception.
Pipes are unidirectional precisely so that filters never collaborate. The moment they do, the clear separation of concerns is gone and you have a monolith with extra ceremony.
Restructure: the filters are probably too complex.
Bidirectional need is usually a symptom that functionality is demarcated wrongly, or that one filter is doing more than one thing.
Accept that this is the wrong style here.
Also a legitimate answer. Back-and-forth communication is one of the two explicit *when not to use* signals for this style.
sections.verdict: The other risks live in the same place. **Overloaded filters** turn a pipeline into an unstructured monolith — governance here is largely about tagging each filter with its type (`@Filter(FilterType.TRANSFORMER)`) so developers can see the role they are about to violate. **Error handling** is genuinely hard: once a pipeline is running, exiting and recovering cleanly is difficult, so identify the fatal conditions *before* defining the architecture. And every pipe is a **contract** — changing one needs strict governance and testing so downstream filters don't break.

sections.t: You need scalability. Distribute the filters?
sections.alt: Four filters in sequence, three of them writing to their own databases
sections.sit: The pipeline works, but elasticity, scalability and fault tolerance all rate one star because it deploys as a single unit. Each filter could be its own deployment unit, with pipes as remote asynchronous calls.
opts: Distribute it. Each filter becomes a service or a lambda.
Elasticity, scalability and fault tolerance all improve substantially. On AWS this is literally a Step Function with one lambda per filter; filters can equally be containers or serverless functions.
You keep the two things this style is chosen for — low cost and simplicity — and you keep the one-star operational ratings that come with a single deployment unit.
sections.verdict: There is no third answer here, and that is the lesson. **Distributing raises the operational characteristics and lowers cost and simplicity, in direct proportion.** This is the classic trade-off of software architecture appearing in its cleanest form: the same architecture, two deployment choices, and the scorecard simply moves along one axis.

sections.t: Characteristics, and when to reach for it
sections.alt: Architecture characteristics ratings for the pipeline style
sections.cap: Every one-star rating here is a consequence of monolithic deployment, and every one of them is buyable.
items: **Use it** for systems of any complexity with distinct, ordered, deterministic one-way processing steps — and where the time frame and budget are tight.

**Don't use it** where you need high scalability, elasticity or fault tolerance without distributing; where filters need back-and-forth communication; or for **non-deterministic workflows**. Faking those with lots of tester filters overcomplicates a simple style and damages maintainability, testability, deployability and therefore reliability.

**Team topologies: it fits all four.** Enabling teams in particular do well here — a specialist can add a transformer after the Time Series Selector to try alternative analysis, using the same data, without disturbing the existing flow.
sections.p: You have already used this style whether or not you named it. EDI tools build document transformations as pipes and filters; database ETL tools move and modify data the same way; orchestrators and mediators like Apache Camel pass information from one business-process step to the next; and MapReduce follows the same topology.

source: Fundamentals of Software Architecture: An Engineering Approach, 2nd ed. — Mark Richards & Neal Ford (O'Reilly, 2025). Chapter 12: Pipeline Architecture Style, pp. 181–192. The Knuth/McIlroy story comes from Jon Bentley's “More Shell, Less Egg”.
